questions.q: Per this lesson, what does a managed cloud container service add on top of an image already sitting in a registry?
options: It rewrites your Dockerfile to use a smaller base image
It pulls the image, runs a container from it, gives that container a public URL, and restarts it if it crashes
It converts the image into a different container format automatically
It replaces the need for a container registry entirely
questions.explain: A registry just stores the image. The managed service is what actually runs it, routes traffic to it, and keeps it alive.

questions.q: The 'configure the build' screen (runtime, build command, start command, port) maps most directly to which earlier lesson's content?
options: Lesson 6's container registry push
Lesson 9's environment variables and secrets
Lesson 3's Dockerfile RUN and CMD instructions
Lesson 11's GPU-enabled containers
questions.explain: The guide calls this out directly: build/start commands and the runtime are the same facts as a Dockerfile's RUN and CMD, just entered as form fields.

questions.q: On the 'configure the service' screen, which two settings does this lesson say matter most once real traffic shows up?
options: The service name and the build command
The port number and the runtime version
The container registry URL and the image tag
The autoscaling policy and the health check endpoint
questions.explain: Autoscaling decides when to add instances; the health check decides whether an instance is alive and should keep receiving traffic — both matter once there's real load.

questions.q: What does a service's 'default domain' refer to, in this lesson's deploy walkthrough?
options: The real, public HTTPS URL the platform assigns once the service is running
The internal-only hostname used for container-to-container traffic
The name of the Dockerfile used to build the image
A placeholder URL that must be manually replaced before going live
questions.explain: Once the service reaches 'Running,' the console shows a default domain: a real public URL someone else can call.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what do AWS App Runner, ECS on Fargate, Google Cloud Run, and Azure Container Apps have in common?
options: They are all exactly the same product rebranded for each cloud
Only one of them actually supports deploying a Docker image
They require completely unrelated configuration with no shared concepts
They're different products that all ask you to configure a build and a service, following the same underlying pattern
questions.explain: The lesson's point is that the two-screen pattern (build config, then service config) repeats across all four vendors, even though the console UI and names differ.
